paragraphs: I shoot on a Pentax K1000 that my uncle left in a closet in 1998. Fully manual. No meter that works. I have taken roughly nine hundred photographs on it and maybe forty are good.

Film costs money, which is the whole pedagogy. Thirty-six frames per roll, nine dollars a roll, six dollars to develop. That is forty-two cents a photograph before you have taken it. You do not spray. You stand there and you wait and you think about whether this is the one, and then usually you decide it is not, and you walk on.

My best picture is of my grandfather's hands on a steering wheel. He is not driving. The car is parked and he is just sitting there and it is 6:40 in the evening in September and the light came through the windshield in a particular way for maybe ninety seconds. I got two frames. One is blurred.
I am applying to study architecture. The connection is light, mostly, and the discipline of forty-two cents. I would like to build rooms where the six-forty light does something.
I scored a 4 on the AIME in tenth grade. Out of fifteen. I had told approximately everyone in my life that I was going to qualify for the USAMO.

The specific problem I want to tell you about is number six. Combinatorics, a counting problem about lattice paths, and I spent thirty-one minutes on it. I know it was thirty-one because I was tracking my time on the back of the sheet, which is a thing I did because a book told me to. Thirty-one minutes and I did not get it and I also did not abandon it, which was the actual error. Problems seven through twelve were sitting there. Two of them were easy.

For about a year after that I told a story where the test was unfair or where I was sick. Neither was true. What was true is that I had built my whole sense of myself around being the kid who was good at math, and a 4 does not fit inside that, so I spent a year refusing to look at it directly.

Junior year I started keeping a log of how long I spent per problem, with a hard cutoff. It is not glamorous. It is a spreadsheet. My AIME score went to 9, which is still not USAMO, and I have made peace with the sentence "I am pretty good at math" instead of the other one. I want to study mathematics anyway. I think you should be allowed to love a thing you are only pretty good at.
I have never been on stage. In four years and eleven productions I have been in the booth, on a ladder, or under the deck, and I would like to make a case for that being the better seat.

My job senior year was lighting design, which sounds artistic and is about seventy percent inventory. We have forty-one working instruments and eleven that are dead in a way nobody has diagnosed. I spent September with a clipboard and a multimeter. The design happens later and only inside the constraints of what actually turns on.

The best moment of my high school career happened during a Thursday preview of Our Town when a follow spot failed in the third act, and I had ninety seconds to re-plot a cue on the board from memory, and I did it, and eleven people noticed and one hundred and forty did not. The eleven were the crew. That ratio is the entire job. If the audience notices your work, something has gone wrong.

I want to study electrical engineering. People assume that if you like theatre you want to be seen, and I have found the opposite in myself. I want to build the thing that makes the seen thing possible and then stand in the dark at the back and watch it work.
I have tutored the same student, a girl named Marisol, for two and a half years. She was in fifth grade when we started and she could not subtract across zeros.

The first six months were a failure and it was my fault. I explained borrowing the way it had been explained to me, with the little crossed-out numbers, and she nodded and then got it wrong, over and over, and I got quietly frustrated in a way I hope she did not notice. Then in November I asked her to show me what she thought the crossed-out number meant. She said it meant "the number is tired." She had built an entire consistent theory out of a notation nobody had explained.

So we threw it out and used dimes and pennies for three weeks. It was slow and slightly humiliating for both of us and it worked completely. She is in eighth grade now and she is in the accelerated math track, which she will tell you about immediately if you give her an opening.

The lesson I actually took is that when someone does not understand something, they are usually not empty — they are full of a wrong model, and you have to find the wrong model before anything else. I want to study education policy. There are a lot of tired numbers in this country and most of them never get asked what they think the notation means.
I broke my wrist twice on the same trick. Kickflip down a four-stair at the Presbyterian church, September and then again in March. The second time the ER doctor recognized me.

I want to be careful here because the obvious version of this essay is about resilience and I do not actually think I was resilient. I think I was stubborn in a way that was close to stupid. Nobody needs to land a kickflip down four stairs. There is no scholarship. My mom cried the second time, which was worse than the wrist.

What did change is that I got interested in why. After the second cast I spent a lot of the spring reading about wrist fractures and load, mostly on my phone, mostly badly. But I learned the difference between a scaphoid and a distal radius fracture, and I learned that you are supposed to fall on your forearms and roll, which is a technique, which is teachable, and which nobody at that park had ever taught anybody.

So I taught it. Not formally. I just started telling the twelve-year-olds at the church, and now there is a whole crew of kids who fall correctly and think it is normal. I want to study kinesiology. It started as an injury and became a curiosity, and I would rather be honest about that order than pretend I planned it.
I have sold four hundred and six pairs of shoes on the internet. Gross revenue was about thirty-one thousand dollars. Net was closer to four, which is the part of the story that taught me something.

It started with one pair. Jordan 1s, a size 11, bought for retail because I got lucky in a raffle and sold three weeks later for two hundred over. I was fifteen and I thought I had discovered a machine. So I scaled it, which for a fifteen-year-old means putting every dollar you have back in, and by sixteen I had roughly sixty pairs in a stack in my closet and my mother could not open the door all the way.

The problem was that I was not tracking anything. I had a vague sense of doing well. Then in January of junior year I actually sat down with a spreadsheet for four hours and put in every fee — platform fee, payment fee, shipping, the two pairs that got lost, the six pairs I bought that never moved and are still in that closet — and the real margin was about thirteen percent, not the forty I had been telling people. Some of those pairs I had sold at a loss without knowing.

I still do it, smaller and better. I keep books now. I want to study accounting, which I am aware is the least romantic sentence in this application. But there is a specific feeling in finding out that your own confident story about yourself was off by a factor of three, and I would like to be the person who checks.
For two years I am volunteer in adult English class at community center on Saturday mornings. Most students are older than me. Some are older than my parents.

I came from Guatemala when I was ten so my English is now good, but I remember, and this is why I do it. There is man in the class, Don Efraín, who is sixty-three and who works in construction and who has lived here for nineteen years without learning to read English. He can speak enough for the job site. He cannot read a letter from the school about his granddaughter.

Teaching adults is completely different from what I expected. Children are not embarrassed. Adults are extremely embarrassed, all the time, and most of the work is not the grammar, it is making the room a place where a man who supervises eleven people can say "I do not know this word" out loud. We spent one entire Saturday on the word "invoice." It was not wasted time.

I want to study public policy. I have watched nineteen years of a person's life be shaped by a reading level, and I have also watched him learn to read a school letter in fourteen months, which means it was never impossible, only unattended. I would like to work on the unattended things.
We lost the roof over the back bedroom in 2022. Not the whole roof — a section maybe eight feet by ten, which was enough. The rain came in for two days before anyone could get up there.

For five weeks nine of us lived in my grandmother's three-bedroom house in Kenner. My cousins, my aunt, us. I slept on a loveseat that was too short and I remember being angry about the loveseat specifically, which in retrospect was a way of not being angry about the larger thing.

What I did during those weeks was run the phones. My parents' English is fine but insurance English is not English, and I was the one who was seventeen and could sit on hold for fifty minutes without losing my temper. I learned the phrase "adjuster's supplement." I learned that if you ask for a claim number at the start of every call you save yourself twenty minutes. I filled a legal pad. We got the payout in March, which was late, and less than it should have been, and more than my aunt got.

I am going to study insurance and risk management, which is a strange thing for a teenager to want. But I sat in that hallway with a legal pad and watched the difference between a family that had someone to make the calls and a family that did not, and it was measured in thousands of dollars, and I have not been able to stop thinking about it.
The bakery starts at 11 p.m. I worked Fridays and Saturdays for a year and a half, which meant my weekend social life happened between 4 p.m. and 10:30 p.m. and then stopped.

Bread is a clock. That is the thing I did not understand going in. You do not decide when to shape the loaves — the dough decides, and it decides based on the temperature of a room you do not fully control, and if you are twenty minutes late the crumb is wrong and a hundred and forty baguettes are mediocre. My boss, Farida, can tell by pressing one finger into a mass of dough. I got to where I could tell maybe seventy percent of the time.

There is a specific quality to the middle of the night in a working room. Nobody talks much. The radio is on low. At about 3 a.m. there is a stretch where everything is proofing and there is genuinely nothing to do for eleven minutes, and Farida and I would stand in the alley and she would smoke and tell me about Algiers.

I want to study food science. I have also had a year and a half of experience being tired in a way that has a purpose, and I know the difference now between that and being tired for no reason, and I suspect that distinction will matter more in college than the chemistry will.
I have a life list of two hundred and eleven species and I keep it in a notebook and also, redundantly, in eBird, because I do not trust myself.

This started as a thing I did with my dad and became a thing I do alone, mostly at the retention pond behind the Home Depot, which is not scenic and which is, ecologically, surprisingly good. Shorebirds stop there. In August of last year I found a Baird's sandpiper, which is a genuinely uncommon bird for our county, and I was so unsure of the identification that I did not report it for four days.

That hesitation is the interesting part. Birding has a peer review culture — you submit a rare sighting and a regional reviewer emails you and asks, politely, how you eliminated the other options. I got that email. I had to write three paragraphs about wing projection and leg color to a stranger. I was wrong about one detail and right about the bird.

I want to study ecology, and I would like to say that what birding gave me is not a love of nature, which I already had, but a habit of asking myself how I eliminated the other options. That email lives in my head now. It asks pretty good questions.
I failed the road test three times. Once for a rolling stop, once for the parallel park, and once — this is the good one — for putting the car in reverse while the examiner was still buckling.

I have an anxiety thing. It is diagnosed and managed and I am not going to make it the centerpiece of this essay, but it is relevant, because the reason I failed three times is not that I cannot drive. I can drive. I could drive at fifteen in an empty church parking lot with my sister in the passenger seat, competently and even a little smugly. I cannot drive while being evaluated by a stranger with a clipboard, or I could not.

The fourth time I passed, and the thing that changed was extremely unglamorous: my therapist and I built a script. Four sentences I say to myself at the curb before the examiner gets in. It is embarrassing to write down. It worked on the first try after failing three times, which suggests the problem was never the parallel park.

I am telling you this because I expect college to contain a lot of rooms with strangers evaluating me. I now know something specific about myself in those rooms, and I know that the fix is a script and not a personality transplant. That is a more useful thing to bring than a clean driving record.

My science fair project on microplastics in local creek water did not find microplastics in local creek water. I want to lead with that because the poster did too, and I think it is the only interesting thing about the project.

The hypothesis was reasonable. There is a plastics processing facility about two miles upstream of Miller's Creek and I expected to find elevated particle counts downstream of the outflow versus upstream. I collected forty-eight samples over eleven weeks, filtered them, and counted particles under a stereoscope at 40x, which took approximately forever and destroyed my back.

The counts were basically identical. Upstream mean 3.1 particles per litre, downstream 3.4, and when my mentor showed me how to actually test that, the difference was nowhere near significant. My first instinct — and I am not proud of this — was to look for a way to slice the data that would show something. I spent a bad weekend doing that. Then I stopped, and I wrote it up as a null result, and I put the effect size and the confidence interval on the poster in large font.

I did not place. A project two tables down that showed a dramatic effect with six samples and no controls got second. I thought about that a lot. I want to study environmental science, and I have decided that I would rather be the person with the boring interval than the person with the ribbon, though I will admit that took me most of a summer to actually mean.
Every Ramadan our mosque packs food boxes and every year for six years I have been on the assembly line, and for the last two I have been the person who decides what goes in the box.

That decision is harder than it sounds. We had been packing the same box since before I was involved: rice, lentils, oil, dates, canned tomatoes, pasta. It is a good box. But in 2023 I started actually asking families what they used, which nobody had done in a systematic way, and about a third of the pasta was going untouched because a lot of our families are Somali and Yemeni and pasta is not what they cook.

So I changed it, and I want to be honest that I changed it badly the first time. I swapped pasta for a spice mix I thought was universal and it was not, and one auntie told me, very kindly and very devastatingly, that I had bought the wrong kind. The second year I put a checkbox on the intake form. Now there are three box variants and almost nothing comes back.

I want to study operations research. I know that sounds like an odd landing after a paragraph about spice, but a food box is a supply chain with a human on the end of it, and I learned that the most expensive mistake in that chain is assuming you already know what people need.
Two winters ago I hired my first employee, who was my friend Dev, and I paid him forty percent of a driveway, and he quit after eleven days because forty percent of a driveway is not very much money.

The business was shoveling. Fifteen dollars for a single, twenty-five for a double, forty for a double with a walk and a stoop. I had nine regulars by the second winter and I cleared about eleven hundred dollars in a season, working entirely on days when school was cancelled, which is the beautiful arbitrage at the heart of the whole thing.

Dev quitting taught me the actual lesson. I had set his cut based on what felt generous to me and not on what the work was worth to him, and I had never asked. When he told me why he was done he was not even angry, he just said the math, and the math was correct and I had never done it from his side.

I raised it to sixty for the next guy. Made less myself. I want to study business, and I would like to note that the useful part of this story is not that I ran a business at sixteen but that I underpaid someone at sixteen and found out about it in a way I could not talk my way out of.

Our dog Pepper died in April of my junior year. She was fourteen, which is old for a beagle, and it was not a surprise, and I still had to leave a chemistry test twenty minutes early because I could not stop crying at a desk.

I am aware that a dog is a small grief in the scheme of it. My grandfather died when I was eight and I remember being confused rather than sad. Pepper I felt entirely, which I have thought about, and I think it is because she was the one constant physical presence of my whole conscious life and my grandfather was a man I saw at Easter.

What I did with it was strange and I am going to include it because it is true. I made a spreadsheet. Every photograph of her we had, dated, with where it was taken, four hundred and eleven rows. It took two weeks of evenings. My father thought I had lost my mind and then he sat with me for one of the evenings and told me things about 2011 that I had not known.

I want to study statistics, and yes, I have noticed that my response to the worst month of my life was to build a dataset. I have decided that is not avoidance. Making a thing countable is one way to hold it.

We run four hundred head of dairy cattle outside Dodgeville and I have milked in the morning since I was eleven. Milking is at 4:30 and again at 4:30, which is a joke my father makes and which is also just the schedule.

People at school think farm work is picturesque. It is mostly manure and repetition and a very specific kind of cold that gets into the metal and then into you. But there is skill in it that nobody outside sees. I can tell a cow is going lame two days before it is obvious, from the way she loads her left rear coming into the parlor. I did not learn that. I absorbed it, over eleven thousand milkings, and I cannot fully explain it to you, which bothers me.

The reason it bothers me is the reason I want to study animal science. We lost eleven animals in 2023 to a herd health problem that took the vet six weeks to name, and during those six weeks I had a hundred observations in my head that I could not turn into evidence because I did not have the language or the records. Feel is not transferable. Data is.

I am the first in my family to apply anywhere. My father is supportive in a way that is mostly silence and one comment in a truck in November. I intend to come back. The farm is a business with a four-decade horizon and I would like to be the generation that writes things down.
I sing second alto in a choir where the median age is somewhere around sixty-four. I have been the youngest member for six years and I will be the youngest member when I leave.

The choir is not good in a technical sense. We have eleven people on a good Sunday, no tenors at all since Mr. Whitcomb's knees stopped letting him drive, and the organ is a half step flat in the winter. But there is a thing that happens in the second verse of a hymn everyone has known for fifty years where the sound stops being eleven voices, and I have never gotten that in a school ensemble with four times the ability.

My actual job in there, unofficially, has become the alto line for people who cannot read music. Three of the altos learned by ear over decades. So on Thursdays I sit at the piano and play their line, over and over, and they sing along, and then on Sunday they have it. This takes about forty minutes a week and it is the reason the alto section exists.

I want to study music education. I have had access to a very good high school music program and I have also seen what happens in a room with no resources and eleven determined people, and I have come to think that the second room is where most of the teaching in this country actually happens.

My grandmother does not use smartphone. She is seventy-nine and she lives in Chennai and we call on Sunday, and for three years the calling was problem because she could not manage the video application on tablet my uncle bought.

So I made program. It is not impressive program — it is Python script on Raspberry Pi connected to old monitor, and it does exactly one thing, which is that at 7:30 on Sunday evening her time, it rings, and there is one large green button, and she presses it, and we are talking. There is no menu. There is no login. I removed everything.

The difficult part was not the code, which took maybe two weekends. The difficult part was watching her use it in December when I visited. I had made the button green and put it in center of screen and I was very proud, and she reached for the monitor, because she did not know that the button was on the screen and the mouse was on the table. This is completely obvious mistake now. I had never once considered it.

Now the button is physical. It is a real button, from arcade parts, and it is red because green in her mind means nothing and red means important. I want to study computer science and I want to work on accessibility. Every assumption I had was wrong and it took one afternoon in December to find out, and I think most software is built by people who never had that afternoon.
